content: Shigella dysentery is a relatively common infectious disease that can occasionally result in death on a global scale. While mild cases of the illness are self-limiting and resolve without specific treatment, more severe cases necessitate the use of antibiotics to achieve a cure and to prevent recurrence of the disease. The choice of antibiotics for treatment varies widely, depending on regional differences in bacterial sensitivity, and these medications are not without potential side effects. The primary objective of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of antibiotics in the treatment of Shigella dysentery. To achieve this, a comprehensive search for relevant clinical trials was conducted in June 2009. The databases reviewed included the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials (mRCT). Additionally, conference proceedings were examined for relevant abstracts, and researchers, organizations, and pharmaceutical companies were contacted to identify further studies. The inclusion criteria for this analysis were randomized controlled trials that evaluated the use of antibiotics in treating Shigella dysentery. Four authors, working in pairs, independently assessed the eligibility of the trials, evaluated their methodological quality, and extracted relevant data. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and a random-effects model was employed in cases of significant heterogeneity. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity, focusing on participant age and the percentage of participants with confirmed Shigella infection. A total of 16 trials, involving 1,748 participants and spanning four decades, met the inclusion criteria. These trials reflected varying levels of sensitivity to Shigella isolates. However, seven of the trials were deemed to have a risk of bias due to inadequate allocation concealment or blinding, and 12 trials were found to have incomplete reporting of outcome data. Limited data from one three-armed trial involving individuals with moderately severe illness suggested that antibiotics reduced the number of diarrheal episodes at follow-up. Specifically, furazolidone was associated with a significant reduction in episodes compared to no treatment (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.48, 73 participants), as was cotrimoxazole (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.59, 76 participants). There was insufficient evidence to determine whether any specific class of antibiotics was superior in efficacy for treating Shigella dysentery. The presence of heterogeneity in some comparisons limited the confidence in the results. However, all antibiotics studied were found to be safe. There was inadequate evidence to evaluate the role of antibiotics in preventing relapses of the disease. In conclusion, antibiotics were shown to reduce the duration of Shigella dysentery. To guide empiric therapy effectively, it is essential to maintain regularly updated local or regional data on antibiotic sensitivity patterns for different species and strains of Shigella. Further clinical trials, adhering to standardized guidelines, are necessary to better understand the role of antibiotics in treating severe forms of Shigella dysentery and in populations at high risk of complications.
